title: Six Questions About Assessment
author: Nick Nickhart
summary: Assessment practices in schools require fundamental rethinking, and school leaders face six critical questions that shape their approach. The dominant numerical model of progress creates an illusion of certainty that is undermined by significant reliability problems in both teacher assessment and standardized testing. An emerging alternative frames the curriculum itself as the progress model, where children keeping pace with a well-sequenced curriculum are making progress. The author concludes that progress is not reliably measurable, a position with significant implications for governance and accountability. Formative assessment and responsive teaching remain the most important practices for classroom teachers, while leaders need separate frameworks. Questions about teacher assessment bands and standardized tests further complicate the picture, as statutory categories have skewed school culture in counterproductive ways.
points: The dominant numerical model of progress creates an illusion of certainty that is undermined by significant reliability problems in both teacher assessment and standardized test data.
An emerging alternative frames the curriculum itself as the progress model: if children keep pace with a well-sequenced, iterative curriculum, they are making progress.
The author concludes that progress is not measurable in a reliable sense, a position with significant implications for governance structures and how leaders report to governors.
Formative assessment and responsive teaching remain the most important assessment practices for classroom teachers, while leaders need separate frameworks to monitor school-wide learning.

Statutory three-band assessment categories (working towards, expected, greater depth) have become deeply embedded in school culture in ways that distort thinking about what children are actually learning.
quotes: A numerical progress model gives the illusion of certainty when in fact there are huge reliability issues with the data that underpins a numerical progress measure, whether it is teacher assessment (because of bias, or conflating learning and performance) or standardised test results (because no standardised test matches what’s been taught).
The emerging narrative is that the curriculum is the progress model, that if children are keeping up with a well sequenced, iterative curriculum, they are making progress.
In my experience, the closest we can get to measuring progress reliably is through the model of comparative judgement.
Formative assessment/ responsive teaching is the most important form of assessment that teachers do. That’s fine for teachers, but what about leaders?
Numerical models of progress sought to provide leaders with summaries but they were misinterpreted as absolute truth.
Standardised tests can never assess a school’s unique curriculum so using it to judge whether children have learned what they’ve been taught is nonsense.
Whatever assessments leaders decide to use, they have to fully understand the benefits and limitations, which I’ve tried to capture here
